analysis.one_liner: Makes it illegal to run food ads with nutrition claims that wouldn't be legal on the food label itself.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in a House subcommittee until Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made food advertising subject to the same truth-in-labeling rules that apply to food packages. Ads bragging about low cholesterol would have to disclose fat levels, ads touting fiber would have to disclose total fat, and any nutrition claim would have to carry the phrase "See product label for complete nutrition information." It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to a subcommittee, and no further action was ever taken before the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers shopping for healthier foods. The bill would have stopped advertisers from highlighting one flattering number (like low cholesterol) while hiding less flattering ones (like high saturated fat), so shoppers could compare products on the full picture rather than a cherry-picked claim.

how_it_helps.text: The bill deems any food ad misleading if it makes a nutrition or health claim that does not meet the standards required for on-package labeling under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.

It specifically requires advertisers to disclose saturated fat when a claim highlights cholesterol, disclose cholesterol when a claim highlights saturated fat, and disclose total fat when a claim says the food is high in fiber — closing the most common ways a technically true claim can still mislead.
Any ad making a nutrition claim would have to clearly and conspicuously state "See product label for complete nutrition information," steering consumers to the full facts.

analysis.who_pays: Food manufacturers and food advertisers, who would face Federal Trade Commission enforcement if their ads made nutrition claims that the underlying labeling rules would not allow, plus the cost of reviewing and rewriting ad claims.
analysis.who_pays_short: Food makers and their ad agencies

drawbacks.text: The bill applies a strict liability-style standard: an ad is "deemed misleading" if it fails the labeling rules, which could expose advertisers to FTC action even where the underlying claim was true, and compliance review costs would fall on smaller food companies as well as large ones.

It adds a second regulator to nutrition claims — the FTC on the advertising side and the Department of Health and Human Services on the labeling side — and its effective date is tied to when HHS labeling regulations take effect, which could create uncertainty for advertisers about which rules applied when.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to consumers is real but modest: it targets a narrow slice of advertising — nutrition and health claims — rather than food marketing as a whole. The compliance cost falls on advertisers, but it mostly requires them to stop making claims the government had already determined were not accurate on the label itself. The bill's main weakness is coordination: it piggybacks on labeling regulations that were themselves still being written.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, passed along to a subcommittee, and never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Joseph Moakley introduced the bill on April 9, 1991.
Twenty House Democrats cosponsored the bill, with additional sponsors added through February 1992, including senior members such as Henry Waxman.
The House referred the bill to the Energy and Commerce Committee on the day of introduction, and on April 22, 1991 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Transportation and Hazardous Materials.
No further action appears in the record: the bill never left the subcommittee and died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Food manufacturers and advertisers are better off: without the law, they kept full freedom to make nutrition and health claims in ads that highlighted favorable nutrient numbers without disclosing less favorable ones.

for.name: Rep. John Joseph Moakley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it for the full two-year Congress.

for.name: 20 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including senior members such as Henry Waxman and Barney Frank.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and never reported it out; it was sent to the Subcommittee on Transportation and Hazardous Materials and no hearing or markup appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: All 21 sponsors and cosponsors in the record were Democrats; no Republican cosponsor appears, and the committee where the bill sat never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would have restricted their ability to advertise foods using nutrition and health claims unless the claims met labeling standards — for example, a low-cholesterol ad would have to disclose saturated fat. Shoppers would get the full nutrition picture, and companies could no longer market around a single flattering number.

Ad agencies and broadcasters handling food accounts would face new FTC-enforced rules on nutrition claims, including a mandatory disclosure line in relevant ads, raising review costs and forcing changes to some campaigns.
